judged_text: The computed schema keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` both evaluate to the same junk string ('[object Object]', the second overwriting the first), so minimumTokenResponseSchema implements neither the 'any numeric property is the expiry' rule nor 'allow other properties' - it is effectively z.object({access_token: z.string()}) that strips every other field from its parsed output. In sharing mode all token fields except access_token are silently discarded before persistence: O365 never receives the new expires_in so the credential's expiry never advances (refresh runs on every operation), and Salesforce's stored key is stripped to {access_token, refresh_token}; no expiry validation ever runs, so any sync response with a string access_token passes.

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts`, `minimumTokenResponseSchema` uses computed keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]`. In JS these evaluate to a single string key (likely `"[object Object]"`), so the second overwrites the first and the schema does not actually accept arbitrary numeric/unknown properties. Since `z.object(...)` strips unknown keys by default, in sharing mode `safeParse(response)` will retain essentially only `access_token` (and possibly the junk key), discarding expiry fields and other token fields. The diff then uses this helper for token refresh flows (e.g., Office365 `CalendarService.ts`, Zoom `VideoApiAdapter.ts`, Salesforce `CalendarService.ts`), meaning refreshed expiry/metadata can be silently dropped before persisting, causing incorrect refresh behavior and overly-permissive validation.
